common_name: Royal Rosa Apricot (Zaiger White-Fleshed Low-Chill Apricot)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Royal Rosa has a low chill requirement of roughly 300 hours, making it one of the few apricots reliable in mild-winter Southern California and similar warm zone 8-9 gardens.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun and avoid frost pockets, since early bloom makes flowers vulnerable to late cold snaps. Royal Rosa is self-fertile and needs no pollinizer, and thinning developing fruit to a few inches apart improves size and prevents limb breakage. It is prized for pale creamy-white to blush-pink skin and sweet, low-acid, aromatic white flesh that distinguishes it from standard orange-fleshed apricots. Its unusually low chill requirement makes it a go-to choice for gardeners in mild-winter regions where Blenheim and Moorpark can bloom unevenly.

common_name: Puget Gold Apricot (Pacific Northwest Maritime Apricot)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained soil in the sunniest available spot; Puget Gold needs about 600-700 chill hours and was specifically bred at WSU Puyallup to bloom later and set fruit reliably in the cool, wet spring conditions of the maritime Pacific Northwest.

directions: Site trees against a south-facing wall or in the warmest microclimate available to maximize summer heat and ripening in cool coastal climates. Puget Gold is self-fertile and was developed at Washington State University's Puyallup research station specifically to succeed where most apricots fail in the region's damp, late springs, thanks to a later bloom period that dodges frost and better tolerance of humid growing conditions. Fruit is medium-large, golden-orange, and freestone with good flavor for a cool-summer climate. Thin fruit after the natural June drop to improve size and reduce limb stress.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Tomcot requires roughly 500-600 chill hours and blooms early, so protect against late frost in marginal zones.

directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and thin fruit after natural drop to prevent overbearing on this heavy-setting cultivar. Tomcot is valued commercially and by home growers for ripening two to three weeks ahead of most other apricots, filling the earliest slot in the harvest season with large, firm, richly colored fruit. It is self-fertile and also serves as an excellent pollinizer for other apricot varieties thanks to its abundant, early bloom. Because it flowers so early, plant in a site with good air drainage to reduce frost damage to blossoms.

common_name: Southern Belle Nectarine (Deep South Very-Low-Chill Nectarine)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Southern Belle needs only about 150-200 chill hours, making it suitable for the mild winters of the Deep South and Gulf Coast where standard nectarines fail to bloom reliably.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Southern Belle is self-fertile and needs no pollinizer. Bred for the Gulf South, it produces yellow-fleshed fruit early in the season, giving warm-climate gardeners a nectarine option where most standard cultivars cannot accumulate enough winter chill to fruit well. Thin fruit after natural drop to improve size, and watch for brown rot and plum curculio, both common challenges for stone fruit in the humid Deep South. It performs best with a regular fungicide program suited to warm, humid summers.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Karla Rose needs only about 300 chill hours, suiting it to mild-winter coastal and Southern California gardens as well as similar warm zone 7-9 climates.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun and thin developing fruit to a few inches apart to encourage larger, sweeter fruit. Karla Rose is prized for white, low-acid, semi-freestone flesh with an intensely sweet, aromatic flavor that stands apart from typical yellow-fleshed nectarines. It is self-fertile and blooms attractively with showy pink flowers in early spring. Because it sets a heavy crop, an annual dormant-season prune helps maintain an open canopy and manageable size for home orchards.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Orlando tangelo is largely self-incompatible and needs a compatible pollinizer such as a Dancy tangerine or Temple orange planted nearby for good fruit set.

directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun, and site a compatible pollinizer citrus within about 50 feet since Orlando sets poorly on its own. This USDA-bred hybrid of Duncan grapefruit and Dancy tangerine, developed in Orlando, Florida, produces medium-sized, deep orange, easy-peeling fruit with juicy, mildly sweet flesh that ripens in midseason, generally ahead of its offspring cultivar Minneola. The tree is vigorous, moderately cold-hardy for a tangelo, and productive once established. It is one of the parent cultivars behind several modern tangelo hybrids but is less commonly planted itself today, making it a good candidate for home orchards seeking classic mid-century Florida citrus.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Citrus Research and Education Center
University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection

common_name: Alstonville Finger Lime (Commercial Australian Caviar Lime Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring; Alstonville tolerates brief frosts to about 25°F once established but grows best where winters stay mild, similar to other finger lime selections.

directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, since this rainforest-understory species tolerates and even benefits from some afternoon protection in hot inland climates. Alstonville is the leading commercial finger lime cultivar in Australia, selected for vigorous upright growth, heavier yields, and consistent production of glossy green, cylindrical fruit filled with pale green caviar-like pulp vesicles. It is self-fertile and bears at a younger age than most finger lime seedlings when grown on grafted rootstock. Harvest when fruit detaches easily with a gentle twist, and use the tangy pulp fresh as a garnish since it does not store well once opened.
sources: New South Wales Department of Primary Industries

common_name: Centennial Variegated Kumquat (Variegated-Leaf Ornamental Sweet Kumquat)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; like other kumquats it tolerates brief cold to the low 20s°F once mature, but is most reliable in mild-winter zones or as a protected container specimen further north.

directions: Grow in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun for the best combination of foliage variegation and fruit color, since strong light intensifies both. This sport of a sweet round kumquat is grown as much for ornamental appeal as for fruit, with cream-and-green variegated leaves and young fruit that displays green-and-yellow stripes before ripening to solid orange, sweet-skinned fruit similar in flavor to Meiwa. It is self-fertile and well suited to large containers, where its compact size and eye-catching foliage make it a striking patio specimen. Bring container plants into a bright, cool indoor spot before hard frost in colder zones.
